name: Detox / slimming teas

card.summary: Herbal teas, often senna-based, sold to cleanse or slim; the weight change is typically fluid, and a 2015 review found no compelling evidence for detox claims.
card.note: Senna-containing teas act as stimulant laxatives; reported effects include cramps, diarrhea and potassium loss.

quick.overview:
Detox or slimming teas are herbal blends marketed for cleansing and weight loss. Many rely on senna, a plant whose sennosides are a stimulant laxative.

A 2015 review of detox diets, summarised by Wikipedia, found no compelling evidence for weight management or toxin elimination, and weight lost on such regimens is typically regained. Few trials of the teas themselves are listed.
quick.mechanism: Senna is thought to increase fluid and electrolytes in the large bowel and stimulate gut movement, so apparent weight change largely reflects stool and water loss rather than body fat.
quick.risks: Reported senna effects are abdominal cramps, diarrhea, nausea and flatulence, and lower potassium, which can increase digoxin toxicity. Regular use can cause melanosis coli, a brown discoloration of the colon wall. Senna is contraindicated in intestinal obstruction and some inflammatory bowel conditions.

lead: Detox or slimming teas are herbal drinks marketed to cleanse the body and help people slim down and look less bloated. Many are built around senna, a plant-derived stimulant laxative, often alongside other herbs [1][2]. People use them in short courses, sometimes called a teatox, in the hope of a flatter-looking stomach, lower scale weight and a leaner appearance before an event or photo.

Senna glycosides raise fluid in the bowel and stimulate movement, typically acting within 6 to 12 hours of an oral dose [2]. Because laxatives act after nutrients have been absorbed, the change in weight they produce is mainly from fluid and bowel contents [3]. Proponents of detox products describe them as clearing toxins; reviewers note the term is rarely defined [1][4].

A 2015 review of detox diets in the Journal of Human Nutrition and Dietetics found very little clinical evidence for them and noted that no randomized controlled trials of commercial detox diets in humans had been conducted [4].

chain: Tea containing senna acts as a stimulant laxative
Bowel contents and fluid are cleared
Abdomen looks flatter and scale weight drops temporarily
angle.text: People drink these teas for a short-term flatter, less bloated look and a lower number on the scale. The effect comes mainly from bowel contents and fluid [3], and regained weight after returning to normal eating is described in reviews of detox regimens [1].

infobox: Varies; senna is an over-the-counter laxative in the US [2]

paras: Detox regimens in general claim that toxins stored in fat are released and eliminated through the skin, urine, feces or breath, and some proponents point to changes in body odor as a sign [1]. Practices range from juice fasting to colon cleansing, and teas are one of the packaged products in this market. Dietitians and toxicologists quoted in reference sources say the liver and kidneys already handle elimination [1].
Teas in this category commonly include senna as the active laxative component [2].

Ideas about internal cleansing have a long history. Reference sources describe colonic autointoxication theories in the 19th century, a decline in the early 20th century, and a resurgence with alternative medicine from the 1970s, later framed around pollution and chemical exposure [1].

Senna glycosides are dimeric anthraquinones thought to increase fluid and electrolyte content in the large bowel and stimulate peristalsis [2]. Laxatives work after the small intestine has absorbed nutrients, so weight changes are mainly water loss [3].

Reported effects of senna include abdominal cramps, diarrhea, nausea, vomiting and discolored urine; regular use can cause melanosis coli, and senna may increase digoxin toxicity by lowering potassium. Contraindications include intestinal obstruction, acute inflammatory bowel disease and appendicitis [2]. Older concerns about colon damage and dependence are described as not supported by current evidence, although high-quality long-term data are lacking [2].

Laxative misuse can cause dehydration and electrolyte disturbances that can be potentially fatal [3]. A 2022 review of fad diets says limited evidence supports their proposed claims and that some carry health risks [5].

The Mayo Clinic's Katherine Zeratsky said in 2012 there is little evidence that detox diets remove toxins [1]. The British Dietetic Association has criticized detox as a marketing term, as reported in reference sources [1]. Proponents describe the teas as a gentle cleanse and a way to kick-start healthier habits.

No studies found on slimming teas as a product category. Broader research includes the 2015 critical review of detox diets for toxin elimination and weight management [4], which reported small studies with methodological limitations, and a 2022 review of fad diets [5]. Senna's laxative effect is established in medical use for constipation and bowel preparation [2].

timeline.event: Walter Alvarez's JAMA article on autointoxication is cited as a turning point away from colon-cleansing theories [1].
Review of detox diets for toxin elimination and weight management published in the Journal of Human Nutrition and Dietetics [4].
